<Rep. Maxine Waters, Rep. Brad Sherman, Rep. Stephen F. Lynch, Rep. Bill Foster, Rep. Joyce Beatty, Rep. Rashida Tlaib, Rep. Sylvia R. Garcia>: H.R. 9330, the Earned Wage Access Consumer Protection Act establishes a disclosure framework for so called ``Earned Wage Access'' advances but does not appropriately include consumer protections to protect the users of such products from abuse, such as any caps on the associated costs. Among other issues, this legislation excludes EWA advances from traditional caps on credit, like state usury caps. Furthermore, any limits on the access to earned wages requested by customers, including the amount of earned wages a consumer can access, how many times a consumer can access their earned wages, and associated fees and tips for accessing earned wages, would be determined by the EWA providers themselves. Moreover, the bill does not address the lack of federal oversight of consumer laws presently, as the Trump Administration continues to try to shutter the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB).
EWA advances offer individuals access to a portion of their earned income, prior to being issued their paycheck at the end of the standard pay period.\22\ EWA providers have varied business models, fee structures, and repayment methods and do not have standardized practices across the industry.\23\ Two major EWA models consist of the direct-to-consumer (D2C) model and the employer-integrated model, also called employer-partnered model.\24\ D2C EWA providers utilize their own funds to execute the advance for the user and typically recover funds by debiting users' checking accounts.\25\ Employer-integrated models are directly connected to the employer's payroll data, which provides information on the user's wages, pay period, and related data.\26\ In various EWA business models, EWA providers can charge workers one or more of the following fees: ``a monthly membership fee, [expedited access fees] for instant access or same-day [deposits,] fee per withdrawal (some EWA apps equate this to an ATM fee), fee per bank transfer, and/or an optional `tip' after each transaction.''\27\ Depending on the EWA product, particularly those that are structured as a subscription service, EWA products could result in consumers ending up in a cycle of consistently accessing their wages before they are actually paid, and accumulating fees and interest in the process. A Harvard study ``found that 40% of the people who had access to an EWA program through their employer were using it at least once a week . . . The survey further found that 60% of respondents had used a business-to-consumer (B2C) EWA app--often more expensive than an employer-sponsored EWA program--and the vast majority of those had used more than one, employing 2.45 apps on average.''\28\ The variety of business models and fee structures used by different EWA providers demonstrates the range of risks consumers may confront in the EWA marketplace, none of which are adequately addressed by this legislation.
EWA risks to consumers are especially heightened with a weakened Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) and the agency's drastically scaled back oversight under the Trump Administration. In fact, this bill restricts the enforcement and oversight of the EWA ecosystem by placing the oversight of EWA providers under the CFPB while ignoring Trump's attempted shutdown of CFPB. The bill does not increase CFPB funding, proscribe CFPB supervision of EWA providers, and nor authorize expanded state authorities or new private rights of action to hold EWA providers accountable.
In addition to not including any meaningful limits or caps on the charges associated with EWA products, this legislation ensures EWA advances are not considered credit, that EWA providers are not considered creditors or lenders, and that fees or tips are not considered interest or finance charges under federal law. Through this language, EWA advances would be exempted from being regulated as credit-like products, and EWA users would not have the range of consumer protections encompassed in the extension of credit. For example, under this legislation, service members would no longer benefit from the Military Lending Act (MLA) 36% rate cap relating to fees and tips they pay for EWA products. This language stands in contrast to court rulings that have concluded that EWA products are, in fact, a form of credit.
Furthermore, as written, Republicans have carved out EWA providers from having to comply with federal civil rights laws and fair lending laws like the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA)--a critical legal protection that addresses systemic discrimination in consumers' access to credit. Republicans have also failed to include any robust protections of users' data in this legislation, although EWA services amass vast consumer financial data, sometimes including worker geolocation data. To make matters worse, while this bill purports to establish rules around tipping, it includes language that would still allow EWA companies to request a tip and encourage users to tip under certain conditions. In the same way that it would be widely considered inappropriate if a banking app were to solicit tips, it is inappropriate for EWA companies to do the same.\29\
During the markup, Democrats offered two amendments aimed at alleviating the deficiencies within the legislation, but both were rejected by Republicans.\30\
• Ranking Member Waters' amendment establishes
a monthly $10 limit on fees and tips that an EWA
provider can charge or solicit from a consumer in
connection with EWA services.
• Rep. Pressley's amendment would ensure that
this bill does not preempt the consumer protections and
other provisions of State laws governing EWA services.
H.R. 9330 is opposed by 226 labor, consumer, civil rights, and community organizations.\31\ For these reasons, we oppose H.R. 9330.
Sincerely,
Maxine Waters,
Ranking Member.
Brad Sherman,
Stephen F. Lynch,
Bill Foster,
Joyce Beatty,
Rashida Tlaib,
Sylvia R. Garcia,
Members of Congress.
